$meta.name: JRK Analytics Design Tokens
$meta.description: Single source of truth. Run `npm run build` to regenerate dist/. Never hand-edit dist/.
$meta.look: Soft modern web UI on an Apple colour foundation. White cards floating on a #f5f5f7 page with ambient shadow, pill-shaped controls, generously rounded tiles, tall chrome. The COLOUR layer is unchanged and still Apple — system greys, the reserved status colours, the CVD-derived chart palette, and the stepped-blue accent at hue 212deg (#0069d9, deeper than systemBlue, which fails both as a button label and as link text). What changed on 2026-08-13 is geometry, elevation and the page plane; not one measured colour moved, and the accent is the same blue it has been.
$meta.$lookNote: Read this before 'restoring' anything to macOS. The tight radii, the flat page and the no-resting-shadow rule were coherent and are gone on purpose — the brief moved from 'this should feel like a Mac app' to 'this should feel like a modern web product', and several notes in this file argue for the old geometry using 'Apple does it this way' as the premise. Those arguments are preserved where they are, marked, because the MEASUREMENTS in them are still good and only the premise expired. Anything justified by a contrast ratio, a CVD deltaE or a WCAG floor is untouched and is not up for restyling.
$meta.$surfacesNote: This is the surface `validate` measures EVERY dark check against, so it has to track color.surface.default or the whole gate quietly drifts. It sat at #1c1c1e after the card was lifted to #232326 and nothing noticed, because a validator cannot check its own constant: every dark contrast ratio was reported against a card that no longer existed, ~8% high across the board. Re-measured on correction and nothing failed — the leniency was never load-bearing — but it was measuring the wrong thing for as long as it was wrong. If surface.default.dark moves again, move this with it in the same commit.
$meta.$surfaceNote: LIGHT does not separate its planes by fill: page and card are both #ffffff, so .jrk-card draws a border.subtle HAIRLINE (1.26:1) and that is the tile boundary. DARK keeps the Apple grouped fill hierarchy (#141416 page, #232326 card, 1.17:1) and draws the same hairline on top of it, where it is additive rather than load-bearing (1.24:1). One mechanism, per-theme values. NOTE this note itself was stale for a long period — it described a 2px border.card edge that no longer exists and a #1c1c1e dark card that had been lifted — which is exactly the failure mode the canvas $lightNote warns about: prose and value drifting apart. The chart surface is the CARD in both modes (#ffffff light, #232326 dark); in light that is numerically identical to the page but is a different fact, and marks are measured against the card.
$meta.$appleNote: Values are Apple's system colours verbatim wherever they clear WCAG. Where Apple's own value fails — systemGray as body text is 2.92:1, three of four status marks are under 3:1 on light — the token is darkened and the deviation is noted on the token.
$meta.validated: Categorical palette passes the dataviz six-checks in both modes on both pairlists. Run `npm run validate` after any color change.

ramp.$comment: Apple system greys and the systemIndigo family. Semantic tokens below reference these; components never reference a ramp step directly.

neutral.$comment: systemGray6 -> systemGray, then the dark-mode greys. Light half is Apple's light system greys; 700 and below are Apple's dark system greys.

color.$comment: Semantic color tokens. Every entry has a light and dark value; dark is SELECTED for the dark surface, never computed from light.

surface.$comment: The light page is FLAT #ffffff and dark keeps the Apple grouped fill step (#141416 page / #232326 card, 1.17:1). Because light has no step, the tile boundary is a border.subtle hairline drawn by .jrk-card in BOTH themes — 1.26:1 in light where it does the whole job, 1.24:1 in dark where it is additive. That is deliberately ONE mechanism with per-theme values rather than hairline-in-light / fill-in-dark: two mechanisms is the shape that lets a change read correctly in one theme and vanish in the other, which this library has already paid for once. canvas.light and that hairline are a PAIR — see the $lightNote on canvas for the rule and the history. What lifts an interactive tile is still a hover SHADOW in light and a fill in dark; see shadow.md and .jrk-card--interactive.

canvas.$lightNote: #fbfbfb, a WHISPER tint — and the page went #ffffff -> #f5f5f7 -> #ffffff inside 2026-08-13 and to #fbfbfb on 2026-08-16, so read the RULE and not the value: page flat -> the card must draw its OWN edge; page tinted -> the fill step CAN be the edge and the border MAY go transparent. Note the direction of that permission, because this change is the worked example of taking it the SAFE way. Moving off flat white ADDS a step (1.00:1 -> 1.035:1) while every existing edge is kept, so a tile ends up more bounded than it was, not less. The permission this tint grants is therefore DECLINED: 1.035:1 is a whisper, far below the 1.09:1 the #f5f5f7 era gave and the 1.12:1 of #f2f2f7, so it cannot bound a tile on its own and the hairline plus the resting shadow are still doing the entire job. .jrk-card carries border.subtle (1.21:1 on this page, down from 1.26:1 on white) AND shadow.shadowCard, .jrk-topbar carries border.subtle plus the same shadow, .jrk-sidebar carries border.subtle. TREAT THE FILL STEP AS DECORATION, NOT AS A BOUNDARY: any new top-level tile must still bring its own edge. Note also that this is a PURE NEUTRAL (r=g=b), unlike every previous tint here -- #f2f2f7 and #f5f5f7 both carry Apple's cool cast. Nothing measures the difference; it is a look decision, and it means the page no longer shares a hue family with surface.subtle. The history is the argument for the rule. #ffffff first shipped paired with a 2px brand edge doing the whole job of bounding a tile; the edge was later removed and the page was not un-flattened with it, which left light cards at a 1.00:1 step behind a transparent border, i.e. no boundary at all, and it shipped that way. Then #f2f2f7 with the fill step doing the work, then flat #ffffff with a hairline, then #f5f5f7 for the soft-UI refresh, then flat again, and now #fbfbfb with the hairline still carrying it. Every one of those states was internally consistent; the only broken one was the half-finished revert. Never leave one of the two moved without the other. The prose has ALSO been the stale half once: the #f5f5f7 -> #ffffff revert moved the value and left six docs describing a tinted page for three days, so when you move this token, grep the docs for the old hex in the same commit.
canvas.$lightWhyNotF2Note: HISTORY, kept because the constraint outlives the decision. This recorded why the 2026-08-13 tint landed on #f5f5f7 rather than the obvious #f2f2f7. It is live again as of the 2026-08-16 move to #fbfbfb, which clears the constraint from the other side -- it is LIGHTER than subtle rather than deeper, so subtle still recedes below it (1.08:1) and the pin is not under pressure. The reason it could not be #f2f2f7: that value IS surface.subtle, and subtle cannot move. Subtle is pinned from below by text.muted, 4.59:1 on #f2f2f7 and 4.23:1 one step deeper (#eaeaef), so the first deepening puts a table header's own label under the 4.5:1 floor. A #f2f2f7 page therefore forces subtle to EQUAL the page, which is a state this library has already shipped and regretted. So: if the page is ever tinted again, it must not land on subtle — and #f5f5f7 is the value that was solved for last time.
canvas.$darkNote: NOT #000000. iOS grouped dark uses true black, but on a 1920x1080 desktop it produces halation against near-white text and reads as a void rather than a page — macOS window backgrounds sit near #1e1e1e for exactly this reason. #141416 is ramp neutral-925. When the brand edge was removed this value was deliberately LEFT ALONE and the card was lifted instead (see surface.default): darkening the page would have widened the same step while re-opening a halation question that was already measured and settled.

default.$darkNote: Was #1c1c1e (Apple's secondarySystemGroupedBackground), which sat a mere 1.08:1 off the page and leaned on the 2px brand edge to be legible as a tile at all. With the edge gone the fill has to do the whole job, so the card was lifted to #232326 — a 1.17:1 step, which is actually stronger than the light theme's 1.12:1. Lifting the card rather than darkening the page keeps the settled #141416 halation decision untouched. Two tokens had to move with it: surface.disabled.dark, which was #242426 and would now be invisible ON the card, and focus.offset.dark, which names this surface.
default.$darkCostNote: Lifting the card costs contrast for everything drawn ON it, because the card IS the chart surface. Every dark chart series mark lost about 8%: worst case is slot 1 blue (#0a84ff) at 4.66:1 -> 4.30:1, and slots 5 and 6 at 4.83:1 -> 4.45:1. All eight still clear the mark floor and the validator reports no new warnings. Text is unaffected in practice — text.primary is 14.3:1 -> 13.19:1. Recorded because this is the cost side of the trade, and if surface.default is ever lifted again these are the numbers that will run out first. These figures were hand-computed at the time and were, for a period, the only honest ones about dark mode in the repo: $meta.surfaces.dark and chart.chrome.surface.dark were both left at #1c1c1e, so `validate` kept reporting every dark ratio against the OLD card, ~8% high, and could not see it — a validator cannot check its own constant. Both are corrected and gated now. The re-run failed nothing, so the leniency was never load-bearing, but the tightest value in dark is the ordinal floor at 2.16:1 against a 2:1 requirement. That is the one with the least room left.

tinted.use: KPI band, highlighted tiles — soft brand wash. .jrk-card--tinted, .jrk-stat--tinted, .jrk-stat-row--tinted
tinted.$note: REPAIRED 2026-08-14. It was #ffffff light / #0e3543 dark, which is two separate failures wearing one token. In LIGHT it was the card fill verbatim, so `--tinted` was a no-op that had silently done nothing since the page went flat — the exact shape of 'a token that names a plane goes wrong when it becomes EQUAL to the plane it sits on', and the fourth instance of it on record. In DARK it was a saturated teal left over from the #9ee4ff cyan accent two accents ago, on a hue that appears nowhere else in the current file. So the same modifier drew nothing by day and a teal slab by night, which is what a reader reported. Both values are now on the accent's own hue (212deg) and are chosen to be the SAME GESTURE in both themes: a 1.11:1 wash off the card in light, 1.10:1 in dark.
tinted.$inkNote: The light value is pinned from below by text.muted, not by taste. --tinted is a general surface modifier — .jrk-card--tinted can contain anything, including a .jrk-card__subtitle at text.muted — so the floor is 4.5:1 for #6e6e73, which needs relative luminance >= 0.882. #eef4fd measures 4.59:1 and is close to the deepest blue that clears it; accent.wash (#e3efff) is 4.36:1 and FAILS, which is why this is not simply pointed at that token. Dark #0f2b4b holds text.muted #98989d at 4.98:1 and text.primary at 12.04:1.
tinted.$notAccentWashNote: Deliberately not accent.wash, and not only because of the ink. accent.wash means SELECTED — a chosen segment, the current nav pill, a selected table row, the tinted button's fill. A tinted tile is not a selected one, and pointing them at one value would mean a selected row inside a tinted card is invisible. They are close relatives on one hue and that is intended; keep this one the paler of the two.
tinted.$pageNote: The wash reads off the CARD, not off the page: in light it is 1.11:1 against #ffffff and only 1.02:1 against the #f5f5f7 page, so a SPLIT stat tile — which sits directly on the page — is tinted as a hint rather than as a boundary. That is fine and is not the tint's job: the tile is bounded by its own border.subtle hairline and shadow.card. It is the same ceiling surface.subtle documents from the other direction, and it is why deepening this value to 'make the tint show on the page' is the wrong move — it would break the ink floor above long before it bought a boundary the hairline already provides.

subtle.$lightPinnedNote: PINNED. This value cannot deepen: text.muted (#6e6e73) measures 4.59:1 on #f2f2f7 — 0.09 over the body floor — and 4.23:1 on the next step down, so a table header carrying its own muted label goes illegible on the first deepening. It cannot lighten either without giving up the recess off the card. It is a fixed point that other surfaces get chosen AROUND, which is why the 2026-08-13 page tint went to #f5f5f7 rather than to the #f2f2f7 the surrounding design language wanted. That tint was reverted, and the page is a #fbfbfb whisper as of 2026-08-16 — lighter than this token rather than deeper, so it approaches from the safe side. The pin has not moved and does not.
subtle.$lightOnPageNote: Right now this is a recess on BOTH planes — 1.08:1 below the #fbfbfb page and 1.12:1 below the white card — so a table header or an inset well reads as set into whatever it sits on. The page figure is a property of how light the page happens to be and it is NOT durable: through the #f5f5f7 soft-UI period it measured 1.02:1 on the page, i.e. invisible there, while still working correctly inside a card. Every step the page takes toward subtle eats that margin, and 1.08:1 is already faint. Which is the trap, because the failure is silent and one-sided — the component looks right everywhere it is normally tested. Do not build a PAGE-level wash on this token without re-measuring against the page of the day; surface.track is recessed in both themes and is the choice that survives a re-tint.
subtle.$lightNote: #f2f2f7, and with the page at #fbfbfb this is still a genuine recess against both the page and the card, though the page margin is now only 1.08:1. Do not re-derive it from the page: the whole point is that it sits BELOW whatever the page is, which is exactly what stops working when the page tints toward it — see $lightOnPageNote. It has spent one period equal to the page (both #f2f2f7), where it receded from a card but was invisible on the page itself, and an earlier period at #ffffff as the stale half of the flat-page-plus-brand-edge pair. It still does not replace surface.track, which is recessed in BOTH themes — subtle.dark is #2c2c2e, LIGHTER than the #232326 card, so this token is a recess in light and a lift in dark.

track.use: the recessed well of a segmented control — .jrk-btn-group and .jrk-tabs--pills
track.$nearMissNote: The sheet's metric block-head used this for part of 2026-08-12, as the both-themes recess that would break a metric header away from the seam above it (1.09:1 in light, 1.27:1 in dark). It was reverted the same day: the header was wanted LOUD and is now accent.solid with a white label, the workbook's own navy-band idiom. Recorded because the reasoning was sound and the coupling it would have created is the thing to remember — a second consumer here means retuning the segmented well silently moves every metric header in every report. If some future recess wants this token, that is the cost, and the ink it forces goes with it: text.muted is 4.15:1 on this fill in light, under the body floor, so anything textual on it needs text.secondary (8.96:1).
track.$note: Its own token because there is no longer a general one that is recessed in both themes: the track used to be surface.subtle, which was #f2f2f7 in light; the light-page flattening moved subtle to #ffffff, so the well became the same colour as the card it sits on and the control lost its anatomy silently. subtle is back at #f2f2f7 as of 2026-08-07, but that does NOT retire this token: subtle.dark is #2c2c2e, which is lighter than the #232326 card, so subtle is a recess in light and a lift in dark. This one is recessed in both. It briefly had NO consumer, during the period when both segmented controls were runs of joined bordered boxes with no thumb to inset, and it is in use again now that the thumb is back. Recessed by 1.22:1 in light and 1.13:1 in dark — the same order as the card's own fill step, so it reads as an inset without becoming a box. Dark is #18181a rather than #1a1a1c to stay off surface.disabled.dark; the two would otherwise be the same value in different roles. What sits on it now is a TINTED thumb, and the pairing is weak on purpose-by-instruction: accent.wash is 1.05:1 on this in light and 1.20:1 in dark, where the old accent.solid thumb was 4.28:1 and 3.40:1. If a future change wants the thumb to state selection at 3:1 again, this token is not the thing to move — a track dark enough to carry a pale thumb is far darker than Apple's grouped grey and would read as a box. Put the edge back on the thumb instead.

surface.$removedThumbNote: surface.thumb (#ffffff / #48484a) is GONE, along with the white floating thumb it drew. Its own `use` string declared the invariant that killed it — 'must be LIGHTER than the track in both modes' — and in light it had become #ffffff on a #ffffff track: 1.00:1, no step whatsoever, with a 0.5px shadow as the only evidence a segment was selected. That is a signifier failure rather than a style problem, because something DOES depend on seeing which segment is selected, and the same reasoning is already written on border.accent for the tab underline. The fix at the time was to fill the thumb accent.solid with accent.onSolid ink and semibold — three channels instead of a shadow, borrowing the treatment .jrk-nav-item[aria-current] uses for 'this is the active one'. That has since been replaced twice more: first by joined bordered boxes with a border.accent EDGE on a plain fill, then by the same boxes wearing the tinted button treatment — accent.wash fill, accent.washText ink, semibold — with the border.accent edge KEPT, and finally by a thumb in a WELL again: the tinted button lifted out of surface.track (accent.wash + accent.washText + semibold + shadow.md + the faint accent.washBorder hairline), with no accent edge at all. The invariant survived all of it and is the durable part: a reader depends on seeing which segment is selected, so the signal must MEASURE. The shipping thumb SPENDS it, knowingly and by instruction: no channel on it reaches 3:1. What it has that the dead white thumb did not is a hue, an ink change and a weight change, and its fill is 1.05:1 on the light track where surface.thumb was 1.00:1 — so that margin is thin, and it is the whole distance between what ships and what is recorded here as a failure. A neutral or white thumb must therefore not come back: it would not be a restyle, it would be re-committing this bug. The weight step is the only channel that survives greyscale, so treat it as structure. And if the state ever has to be stated at 3:1 again, the fix is one line: border.accent on the thumb rule. What did not survive is 'answer it the way the nav item does': a segment filled accent.solid is exactly as loud as .jrk-btn--primary, and a segmented control's home is the page header where it stands beside one. Selection and action are different questions and the loudest treatment can only answer one of them. If a white-thumb segmented control is ever wanted back, it needs a track dark enough for white to clear 3:1 on it, which is a much darker well than Apple's.

banner.use: sheet title bar — the LEADING heavy band in a dense report, above surface.bannerDeep
banner.$lightNote: Tracks accent.solid: #5856d6 -> #9ee4ff -> #0069d9. It is a DARK surface again in light mode, so text.onBanner and text.onBannerMuted went back to white with it. This is the largest area the accent covers anywhere in the product, which is why it is the token that exposes an accent's lightness fastest — the pastel made the report's heaviest element its palest, and this reverses that. Dark stays neutral #2c2c2e throughout and has never moved.
banner.$noLongerTheOnlyOneNote: This use string said 'the one heavy element in a dense report' until 2026-08-12, when the sheet's per-metric header became a filled band too (surface.bannerDeep). There are now TWO, and the ladder only holds in light: this is 2.31:1 ABOVE bannerDeep there, so the masthead leads on colour as well as on size. In dark this is a grey and bannerDeep is a navy, so the masthead is 1.15:1 BELOW the band it is supposed to lead — an inversion carried knowingly. Correcting it means moving this token's dark value to the anchor and text.onBannerMuted.dark with it: that ink is #a1a1a6, a grey selected for THIS grey, and it is 2.50:1 on the anchor. Neither half works alone.

bannerDeep.use: the per-metric header band in a dense report — .jrk-sheet__block-head, which carries text.onBannerDeep
bannerDeep.$note: A deep navy, ONE value for both themes like accent.solid, because it measures in both: white is 12.08:1 on it, it is 10.83:1 off the light seam and 1.30:1 off the #232326 dark card — a wider step than the card's own 1.17:1 fill step off the page, so it reads as a band in dark rather than as a smudge. #14375e is Excel's 'Blue, Accent 1, Darker 50%', which is what the source AM Report actually draws its metric headers in, and it lands at hue 211.6deg against the brand anchor's 211.0deg — the workbook's navy and this library's blue are the same hue, which is the only reason adopting it needs no apology.
bannerDeep.$whyNotTheAnchorNote: The header was accent.solid (#0069d9) for part of 2026-08-12 and was rejected as too strong, which was the correct read: 28 metric bands in the CTA's own fill spend a signifier that is supposed to mean 'the one action that commits', and in light it made every metric header the same value as the masthead. This is 2.31:1 below the anchor, so the two are unmistakably different bands and accent.solid means one thing again. Deeper was tried too — #0d2947 is 1.06:1 off the dark card, i.e. invisible as a band in dark, and #1f4e79 is only 1.66:1 from the anchor, which blurs the masthead into the metric heads. This value is the one that clears both.
bannerDeep.$name: 'Deep' describes LIGHT mode, where it sits below surface.banner. In dark, banner is #2c2c2e and this is 1.15:1 lighter — see the inversion note on banner. The name is kept because the light ladder is the one a reader sees first, and because renaming it would not fix the asymmetry.

hover.$lightNote: Equals surface.canvas in light, which is correct for a ROW inside a card (it recedes toward the page) and wrong for a whole TILE — washing a white card with the page colour erases the fill step that bounds it. That is what cardHover below exists for; do not use this token on a card.

raisedHover.use: row hover INSIDE a raised surface — menus, the select popup, the daterange list
raisedHover.$note: surface.hover cannot do this job and failed silently for as long as menus have existed: surface.hover.dark and surface.raised.dark are the SAME value (#2c2c2e), so `.jrk-menu__item:hover` painted a menu row with the exact colour of the menu under it and dark mode had no hover feedback at all. Nothing catches this — the validator measures text and marks, never a wash against the plane it washes. This is the same class of trap as surface.cardHover, which exists because surface.hover erases the fill step that bounds a card. Both are surface.hover being wrong for one specific plane. Light is #f2f2f7, identical to surface.hover, because raised.light is #ffffff and the ordinary step works there — the two modes agree by coincidence, not by rule, so re-measure if surface.raised moves. Dark is a 1.140:1 lift off the raised plane, chosen to match the light pair's 1.116:1 rather than to look right in isolation, and it stays 1.077:1 clear of surface.active so hover and pressed do not collapse into each other.

cardHover.use: fill of an INTERACTIVE card while hovered — see .jrk-card--interactive:hover
cardHover.$note: The two themes deliberately disagree about whether this token does anything, because the shadow that accompanies it only works in one of them. In LIGHT it is a no-op (identical to surface.default) and the hover shadow carries the whole affordance — any tint here would pull the card toward the page and dissolve its boundary at the moment it is meant to respond. In DARK the shadow is nearly invisible (a black shadow on a #141416 page, as noted on the shadow tokens), so the fill has to carry it: #2c2c2e is a 1.125:1 lift off the card. One CSS rule, one token, a real affordance in both themes — which is the alternative to branching the stylesheet on theme.

disabled.$darkNote: This token has now been broken twice by a surface.default move, both times silently, because disabled fills are exempt from the contrast gate and nothing checks them. First it was #1c1c1e, identical to the card, so a disabled control on a card had no fill at all. Then #242426 — which is 1.01:1 against the card's NEW #232326, the same bug again. #1a1a1c is chosen the other way round: it RECEDES from the card at 1.109:1, which is what the light pair does (#f2f2f7 on #ffffff, 1.12:1). Matching the light relationship instead of the light direction is what makes it stable — if surface.default moves again, check this token.

text.$comment: Apple label colours where they pass. muted is DARKER than Apple's systemGray (#8e8e93) on purpose — systemGray measures 2.92:1 on the canvas and fails AA as body text. Apple accepts that for tertiary labels; we do not.

primary.$darkNote: Apple's dark label is pure white, and that is the one place the value is adopted and then backed off. #ffffff on the #1c1c1e card measures 15.9:1 and on the old black page 21:1 — far past AA, and the excess shows up as glare and halation on 42px semibold hero figures. #ebebf0 is Apple's own dark secondaryLabel base tint at ~92% white: 14.3:1 on the card, 15.5:1 on the page, still triple the 4.5:1 floor.

secondary.use: supporting copy, labels — Apple secondaryLabel base

muted.use: axis ticks, captions, placeholders — darkened from systemGray to clear 4.5:1

disabled.use: disabled label — decorative only, never load-bearing

link.use: inline links, accent text — tracks accent.text
link.$lightNote: The brand hex, which it was not under the pastel accent. 5.22:1 on the white card and 5.22:1 on the page, because the page is flat #ffffff and the two are the same value. That is a RELAXATION, not a licence: the anchor was originally pinned against a tinted #f2f2f7 page where it measured 4.68:1, and if the page is ever tinted again that becomes the binding surface once more. Do not lighten this value on the strength of the white page alone.

onBanner.$note: White in both modes again, having spent the pastel era as dark ink (#052f3b) in light. It follows surface.banner, which follows accent.solid: the band went from a pale #9ee4ff back to a saturated #0069d9, so the label went back with it. 5.22:1 on the light band, 15.02:1 on the dark neutral one. The two modes agree in direction once more, but for a reason that can lapse again — check this token whenever accent.solid moves.

onBannerDeep.use: labels on surface.bannerDeep — the sheet's per-metric header band
onBannerDeep.$note: Its own token rather than borrowing text.onBanner or accent.onSolid, for the reason recorded on accent.onSolid: .jrk-btn--danger-solid borrowed that one and a red button's ink direction moved every time the accent did. All three are #ffffff today and they are NOT the same fact. This one is 12.08:1 on its band and has room to spare; text.onBanner is 5.22:1 on the light masthead and has 0.72 of headroom. If either band is ever re-stepped, only the ink that measures against it should follow.

onBannerMuted.$lightNote: A near-white tint, not a grey, and the band is why: white on #0069d9 is only 5.22:1, so there is 0.72 of headroom between onBanner and the 4.5:1 floor for this token to be muted INTO. #e8f1fd spends most of it at 4.58:1. It reads as muted next to white, but the light banner is the tightest type pairing in the file — a genuinely grey label cannot pass there. If the banner ever needs a real muted step, deepen surface.banner rather than lightening this.

border.$comment: Apple separators, and now the ONLY border namespace — there is no longer a brand edge on a tile. A card-like tile is bounded by its FILL STEP off the page in both themes (1.12:1 light, 1.17:1 dark), so these values are for internal rules, input borders, popover edges, and the neutral hairline a NESTED tile takes when it has no page to step off. In dark the hairline does more work than in light because the fill steps are shallower there in absolute terms; both dark steps are lifted off Apple's systemGray5/4 for that reason.
border.$removedNote: border.card is GONE, and so is size.cardEdge. It was a 2px #48a9df brand line on every outermost tile — the one deliberate break from Apple in this file — and it existed because the light page had been flattened to #ffffff and nothing else bounded a tile there. The page is tinted again, so the reason is gone with it. Removing the token rather than leaving it unused is deliberate: it was documented as THE brand line, and a dead brand token in the source of truth is an invitation to put it back on something. This is a BREAKING removal for any consumer that referenced --jrk-border-card or --jrk-card-edge directly.

subtle.$darkNote: Was #2c2c2e, which is 1.22:1 on the old #1c1c1e card — a rule that vanished at desktop viewing distance. #333336 measures 1.31:1 on the current #232326 card.

default.use: input borders, popover edges, and the NESTED-tile hairline — systemGray4 / opaqueSeparator
default.$darkNote: Lifted from #38383a for the same reason as subtle.

strong.use: axis, baselines, dividers needing weight — opaqueSeparator

accent.$lightNote: A tab underline is a non-text signifier under WCAG 1.4.11, so it needs 3:1, and something DOES depend on seeing this one (which tab is selected). Under the pastel this token had to carry its own bespoke step (#0096cf, 3.00:1 on the page — barely) because the anchor was 1.40:1. It now takes accent.text unchanged at 5.22:1 on both the card and the flat white page, so the special case is gone. Keep it tracking accent.text rather than re-deriving it: the floor it has to clear is lower than text's, so text is always the safe value.

accent.$comment: A blue brand at hue 212deg, anchored on #0069d9. This is the second replacement: systemIndigo (#5856d6) -> a #9ee4ff cyan pastel -> this. It reverts the inversion the pastel forced. #0069d9 is a SATURATED MID-TONE, so it behaves the way an accent normally does — white sits on it (5.22:1), it reads as text on both light surfaces (5.22:1 card, 5.22:1 page — the same value while the page is flat white; 4.68:1 when the page was tinted), and it clears the 3:1 signifier floor everywhere. The three roles that the pastel had to route around — border.accent, focus.ring, text.link — now all take the anchor itself, which is the whole point of the change. Not Apple's systemBlue: #007aff gives white only 4.02:1 as a label and 3.60:1 as link text on the page, so it fails here exactly the way systemGray and systemIndigo do. #0069d9 is the shallowest step on the hue that clears 4.5:1 in every light-mode role. Dark takes a SELECTED lighter step for text roles (#64b5ff) and keeps the anchor for fills, because a fill and a glyph do not want the same value on a #232326 card.

solid.use: the .jrk-btn--cta fill, and the sheet banner via surface.banner
solid.$note: The brand anchor, verbatim, and the same value in both modes — a saturated mid-tone needs no per-theme selection because its label is white in both. On the dark card it sits at 3.00:1, which clears the non-text floor, so the fill's own boundary reads without a border.

solidHover.$note: Deepens on hover, same direction as the pastel it replaces but for the ordinary reason: a saturated fill darkens under the pointer. White on it is 6.18:1.

solidActive.$note: Deeper again. White on it is 6.87:1, so the label GAINS contrast through the press sequence 5.22 -> 6.18 -> 6.87. The pastel ran the same sequence in the opposite direction (12.15 -> 8.71 -> 7.69) because it was deepening toward its ink rather than away from it.

onSolid.use: label ON the solid accent — WHITE in both modes
onSolid.$note: This token has now been white, then dark ink (#052f3b, for the pastel era), then white again. The rule is not 'white' or 'dark' — it is 'whatever measures against accent.solid', and the value follows the anchor's lightness. It is still NOT text.inverse: text.inverse is #ffffff in light and #000000 in DARK, for the inverse surface, so the two agree in light and disagree in dark. They have been separate facts through all three accents. Do not collapse them. Do not borrow this token as a generic 'label on a filled control' either — .jrk-btn--danger-solid used to, and the red fill silently inherited the accent's ink direction; that is what status.critical.solid/onSolid now exist for.

text.$lightNote: The brand anchor unchanged — this is the first accent in the library's history where the anchor IS the light-mode text value. 5.22:1 on the white card and on the page, which are the same value now that the page is flat. Keep the derivation in mind rather than the number: this anchor was chosen as the shallowest step on the hue clearing 4.5:1 against a TINTED #f2f2f7 page (4.68:1), which is the harder surface. The flat page gives it headroom it did not have; a tint would take it back.
text.$darkNote: #64b5ff is selected, not derived from the anchor — #0069d9 is 3.00:1 on the dark card and cannot be text there. 7.16:1 on the card, 8.41:1 on the page.

wash.use: selected row tint, soft badge fill, .jrk-btn--primary fill, the segmented-control thumb, the current-page pill in .jrk-nav-item / .jrk-sidebar__action, and .jrk-topbar__search
wash.$consumerCountNote: SEVEN consumers, and the count is the thing to watch rather than the value. This token is the library's 'quiet accent' and every new use spends a little of what the previous ones mean — the topbar search joined on 2026-08-13 and put a wash-filled, washBorder-hairlined, washText-inked control a few hundred pixels from .jrk-btn--primary in the same bar, which is the same anatomy at a glance. It survives because width, alignment and a leading glyph separate a 420px field from a button. A THIRD wash-filled control in that bar would not have that defence, and at that point one of them gives up the wash rather than the trio quietly meaning nothing. Same lesson as surface.track's $nearMissNote: a token with one consumer can be retuned freely, and a token with seven cannot be retuned at all.
wash.$note: This is now a BUTTON fill as well as a tint, which raises the bar on it in one specific way: a wash is a fill STEP, not a boundary. It is 1.16:1 on the white card and the same 1.16:1 on the flat white page (it was 1.04:1 when the page was tinted, i.e. all but gone), and in dark it is 1.06:1 on the #232326 card — i.e. all but invisible as an enclosure. A tile can live with that because its CONTENT groups it; a button cannot, because looking pressable is the whole job. That is what accent.washBorder is for, and why the tinted button draws it rather than relying on the fill.

washHover.use: hover on a wash-filled control — .jrk-btn--primary, selected segment
washHover.$note: One step off the wash in the direction each theme expects: darker in light, lifted in dark. The step is 1.09:1 light / 1.13:1 dark, the same order as surface.raisedHover off surface.raised, so it reads as a hover and not as a state change. The binding constraint is the LABEL, which does not change on hover: accent.washText holds 4.89:1 light and 5.98:1 dark on this value. validate gates both.

washActive.use: pressed on a wash-filled control — .jrk-btn--primary, selected segment
washActive.$note: Deeper again, and the press sequence is deliberately the reverse of accent.solid's. On the solid button white GAINS contrast under the pointer (5.22 -> 6.18 -> 6.87) because the fill deepens away from its ink; on the tinted button the fill deepens TOWARD its ink, so washText loses it (5.31 -> 4.89 -> 4.66). #cfe1fd is the last step that still clears 4.5:1 — the next one down (#c9dcfb) is 4.45:1 and fails. So this value is not a taste, it is the floor, and a 'slightly deeper press' cannot be added on top of it. Dark has room and is not near its limit (5.34:1).

washBorder.use: hairline on a wash-filled control, so the tint is not the only thing bounding it
washBorder.$note: Decorative separation, which the conflict register permits below 1.4.11's 3:1 — the LABEL carries the signal here, at 5.31:1 light / 6.73:1 dark, and nothing depends on seeing this line specifically. It exists because the fill alone does not bound the control on every surface it can sit on (see the note on accent.wash). Measured against everything it has to work on: 1.51:1 against its own fill, 1.76:1 on the white card and the same on the flat white page (1.58:1 when the page was tinted), 1.33:1 against washActive light; 1.91:1 / 2.03:1 / 2.38:1 / 1.51:1 dark. Deliberately FAR below border.accent (5.22:1 light, 6.37:1 dark), which is a different job: border.accent means 'this one is selected' on a tab underline or a focused input. It briefly also meant that on a segmented control's selected segment, and no longer does: the thumb wears THIS hairline now, so a chosen segment and an action button share a fill, an ink and an edge, and what separates them is only the well around the one and the page around the other. That is thin, it was directed, and it is recorded rather than defended. Nothing gates this token either way, the border namespace is unchecked, so the figures live here.

washText.$note: Light is stepped deeper than accent.text, not equal to it: the wash is a tint, so text on it has less room than on the white card. The anchor itself lands at 4.49:1 on #e3efff — under the floor by 0.01, which is the clearest possible demonstration of why this token is separate. #005ec4 (the solidHover step) is 5.31:1. Dark reuses accent.text on the deep wash at 6.73:1.

gradient.$comment: Vivid gradient KPI tiles — .jrk-stat--vivid, the saturated band across the top of a dashboard. FOUR tones, each a two-stop ramp. Every stop is a SELECTED value present in both themes (like accent.solid and surface.bannerDeep), because a tile that brings its own saturated fill is its own surface and does not care what is behind it. What it does care about is the WHITE ink it carries, and that is the single constraint the whole namespace is derived from.
gradient.$derivation: Each stop is the most chromatic colour on its OKLCH hue whose ROUNDED 8-bit hex still carries white at 4.5:1 — i.e. relative luminance <= 0.1833 — with chroma capped at C 0.20 (from) / 0.17 (to) so the tones land in Apple's saturation register rather than neon. Hues avoid the two reserved status families: nothing near h30 (red) or h140-155 (green), because a KPI tile in the colour of `critical` reads as an alarm. Two properties fall out and both are load-bearing. (1) The four `from` stops are LIGHTNESS-MATCHED — white measures 4.85 / 4.86 / 5.22 / 4.88 across them — so hue is the ONLY thing that varies down the row. A tone that is a step darker than its neighbours reads as 'this one matters more', which is a magnitude claim nothing in the data supports. `validate` gates the spread. (2) sRGB gradient interpolation cannot exceed its endpoints in luminance — the decode is convex, so lum(mix) <= mix(lum) — which was verified by sampling all four ramps at 101 points: the worst white contrast is always at 0%, the light end. Checking the two stops is therefore sufficient, and that is what the gate does.
gradient.$hueIsNotIdentity: THE IMPORTANT ONE. These four tones are NOT a categorical palette and must never be walked like one. Measured Machado 2009 + CIEDE2000, half the pairs collapse: violet|blue dE 1.9 under protanopia (the same colour), blue|teal 8.5 tritan, rose|teal 7.9 deutan, against the chart palette's floor of 10. That is not a defect to fix, it is the consequence of holding every stop dark enough for white text — the white-safe slice of sRGB is too narrow to also carry eight-way separation. So the rule is the same one that governs chart.tint: legal ONLY where identity is already carried by something else. On a vivid tile that something is the label, which is mandatory, sits in the tile, and is 4.85:1. Assign a tone by the tile's POSITION in the row, never by what the metric means — the moment 'rose = revenue' becomes a convention, colour is doing identity work it cannot do.
gradient.$referenceNote: This shape came from a reference screenshot whose own gradients do not clear white text — its teal is around #2ec7a9, which gives white 2.2:1, and its lightest pink about 3.3:1. The look survives the correction; the palette does not. These tones are the same sweep (rose -> violet -> blue -> teal) at the depth white actually needs, which reads richer and heavier than the reference pastels. That difference is the cost and it is not negotiable downward: the caption on these tiles is 12px.

from.use: vivid tile tone 1, light end (top-left of the 135deg ramp)
from.$note: OKLCH h348 C0.200 L0.577. White 4.85:1, which is also its step off the flat white page and off the white card — on a white ground those three are one number, and they came apart for one day when the page was #f5f5f7 (4.46:1). Off the #141416 dark page it is 3.79:1, and the tone's deep end is 2.60:1 there. A rose, deliberately NOT a red — h348 keeps it clear of status.critical's family so a KPI tile does not read as an alarm.

to.$note: OKLCH h318 C0.170 L0.483. White 7.09:1. Rotated 30deg toward violet rather than merely darkened, which is what gives the ramp its twist; every tone rotates by the same 30deg so the four read as one system.

from.$note: OKLCH h302 C0.200 L0.572. White 4.86:1, matched to rose within 0.01. Near Apple's systemPurple in register (#af52de) but a step deeper, because systemPurple gives white only 3.19:1 and cannot carry a 12px caption.

from.use: vivid tile tone 3, light end — the brand anchor VERBATIM
from.$note: This is accent.solid, not a colour derived alongside the other three. Deriving a fourth blue put it at #0a6ce5, which is the anchor with a rounding error on it — two brand blues one delta apart, in the same product, is the collision the chart palette already carries once and did not need a second time. Taking the anchor also ties the ribbon to the library instead of letting it float. White 5.22:1, already gated by accent.solid + accent.onSolid. Consequence to respect: this tone is EXACTLY the .jrk-btn--cta fill, so a CTA must never sit on a vivid tile — see $noControlsNote.

to.$note: OKLCH h257 C0.164 L0.465 — the anchor's own hue, deepened to the shared 7.14:1 white step. Deliberately NOT surface.bannerDeep (#14375e), which is the obvious reuse and the wrong one: bannerDeep is 12.08:1, five steps past the other three tones' deep ends, so the blue tile would carry visibly more weight than its neighbours and break the lightness matching the whole set depends on. bannerDeep also means something — the metric band in a report — and a second consumer would couple the two.

from.$note: OKLCH h208 C0.092 L0.540. White 4.88:1. Note the chroma: 0.092 against rose's 0.200, and that is a GAMUT fact rather than a choice — the cyan-teal arc of sRGB has almost no saturated volume left below the white-text luminance ceiling. So this tile reads as the quietest of the four no matter what, which is why it goes last in the row and why the reference's bright mint tile is the one thing here that could not be reproduced at all.

to.$note: OKLCH h182 C0.080 L0.453. White 7.07:1. Stops at h182 rather than rotating the full 30deg to h178-ish green: status.good lives at h150 and a KPI tile must not drift toward it.

barDeep.use: the deep end of the .jrk-topbar--blue masthead ramp, and nothing else
barDeep.$note: THE ONE THEME-VARYING VALUE IN THIS NAMESPACE, and the exception is deliberate. Every tone above is identical in both themes because a vivid TILE brings its own surface and does not care what is behind it. The topbar is the one vivid surface that is chrome rather than content: it spans the full top edge of the page, so at night a bar that stays fully saturated across that width is the brightest object on a dark screen and pins the eye to the chrome instead of the work. In light this is gradient.blue.to verbatim, so the light bar is unchanged. In dark it is surface.canvas, and the ramp runs brand blue at the leading edge and dissolves into the page at the trailing one.
barDeep.$hairlineNote: READ THIS BEFORE REUSING IT. In dark this is EXACTLY surface.canvas, so it is 1.00:1 against the page and the trailing half of the bar has no boundary of its own. That breaks the assumption .jrk-topbar--vivid is built on — its comment says 'the bar bounds itself' and sets border-bottom-color: transparent on that basis, which is true of the three-hue ribbon and is NOT true here. So the blue variant puts the hairline back under dark, in shell.css, and the two are a pair: move this value toward the canvas and the border must stay; move it away and the border may go. Same fill-step-or-hairline rule surface.canvas's own $lightNote states, arriving from the other side. It is also why this is not #000000 — a black below the page would separate from it, but by 1.06:1, which buys a boundary nobody can see and loses the dissolve.
barDeep.$inkNote: White is 18.40:1 here in dark and 7.14:1 in light, so the ink is safe by a wide margin at this end. The ramp only ever gets DARKER than gradient.blue.from and sRGB interpolation cannot exceed its endpoints in luminance, so the white-safe check that matters for this variant remains the LIGHT end — gradient.blue.from at 5.22:1, already gated as accent.solid.

topbar.$comment: The .jrk-topbar--brand masthead ramp — a THREE-stop sweep whose two themes are different designs rather than two values of one design. Dark is a saturated bar carrying white ink; light is a PALE bar carrying black ink. Nothing else in this namespace works that way, and the reason is the single constraint the namespace exists to serve: white needs every stop at relative luminance <= 0.1833, and the pale light bar that was asked for spans 0.19 to 1.00. No ink clears 4.5:1 across a range that wide, so the question is not which ink but which ramp — and the answer is one ramp per theme, each carrying the ink that measures on it.
topbar.$measured: HAND-MEASURED, because nothing gates a colour inside a gradient. validate only iterates NAMED colour tokens in ink and mark roles; a stop consumed by linear-gradient() is invisible to it, which is the blind spot this file's own rule about colours in shadows, gradients and data: URLs describes. WCAG 2.1 relative luminance, sRGB. LIGHT ramp on gradient.topbar.ink light (#000000): from 21.00:1, via 11.47:1, to 7.00:1. DARK ramp on gradient.topbar.ink dark (#ffffff): from 21.00:1, via 8.95:1, to 14.84:1. The interior of each segment needs no separate check, for the reason $derivation gives for the four tones: the sRGB decode is convex, so lum(mix) <= mix(lum) and no interior point can fall outside its two endpoints — the worst contrast on a ramp is always AT a stop. Re-measure all six if any one of them moves.
topbar.$restepNote: gradient.topbar.to LIGHT is the one value here that is not what was asked for, and it was re-stepped rather than waved through. The request specified #006fff, whose relative luminance is 0.1859 — white is 4.45:1 on it and black is 3.78:1, so it fails the body floor under BOTH inks. It is the crossover point of the ramp: too dark to carry black, too light to carry white. The bar's trailing third is where the account menu and sign-out live, so that is an illegible corner rather than a cosmetic one. #4d94ff is the same hue two steps lighter, luminance 0.2998, black at 7.00:1. Do not 'restore' the original value without re-reading $measured.

from.use: the leading (0%) stop of the .jrk-topbar--brand ramp
from.$note: A literal white in light and a literal black in dark, which every other stop in this file would be wrong to be. Legal here only because this variant carries theme-specific ink: black on white and white on black are both 21.00:1, so the leading edge is the SAFEST point of either ramp rather than the most dangerous one. What it costs, and why the cost is accepted: in light this is one step off surface.canvas (1.09:1), so the bar has almost no boundary of its own at that end. That is the same fill-step-or-hairline pairing gradient.barDeep's $hairlineNote describes, arriving at the opposite end of the bar — and shell.css answers it the same way, by keeping the hairline on this variant in BOTH themes.

via.use: the middle (52%) stop of the .jrk-topbar--brand ramp
via.$note: Both are the midpoint that was asked for, resolved to a literal rather than left as a color-mix. Light is the sRGB mean of #ebebeb and #d570ff; dark is the mean of accent.solid (#0069d9) and #d90000. Written out because an expression cannot be measured, and this file's rule for a colour nothing gates is to measure it by hand and write the number down. gradient.blue's midpoint stays a color-mix for the opposite reason: it is DERIVED from its own two endpoints, so it cannot drift into being a new selected value. This one IS a selected value and has to be visible as one.

to.use: the trailing (100%) stop of the .jrk-topbar--brand ramp
to.$note: Dark is the requested #002657 verbatim, 14.84:1 under white. Light is re-stepped from the requested #006fff — see $restepNote, and do not undo it without reading that entry first.

ink.use: ALL text and glyphs on a .jrk-topbar--brand bar — the wordmark, the ghost buttons, the account name and the theme control
ink.$note: THE ONE INK IN THIS NAMESPACE THAT IS NOT WHITE, and the variant depends on it. gradient.ink is white in both themes because a vivid TILE brings its own dark surface; this bar brings a pale one in light, where white measures 1.00:1 at the leading edge and 1.83:1 at the middle. Black rather than text.primary light: the two are the same value today, but text.primary is selected against the page and the card while this ink is selected against a gradient, and coupling them would let a future page-driven change to text.primary silently re-ink a masthead that nothing re-measures. shell.css applies it as a LOCAL --jrk-gradient-ink override, so every descendant rule already reading that property follows without being restated.

ink.use: ALL text on a vivid tile — label, value and caption alike
ink.$note: White in both themes, for the same reason accent.onSolid is: the tile brings its own surface, so the ink is measured against the tone and not against the page. 4.85:1 at the worst point of the worst tone.

gradient.$noMutedInkNote: There is deliberately NO gradient.inkMuted, and the absence is the finding. Every other surface in this library has a two-step ink ladder (text.primary / text.muted, text.onBanner / text.onBannerMuted), and a vivid tile cannot have one: its lightest tone holds white at 4.85:1, so the entire budget is 0.35 above the floor. White at 85% alpha over the rose light end measures 3.92:1 and fails; at 60% it is 2.65:1. Anything dim enough to read as secondary is illegal here. Hierarchy on a vivid tile therefore comes from SIZE and WEIGHT only — 12px regular caption under a 36px semibold figure — and if a design ever calls for a dimmed line on one of these tiles, the answer is a smaller line, not a fainter one.

mark.use: the sparkline stroke, the bar fills and the gauge arc on a vivid tile
mark.$note: Solid white, because it is the only value that clears the 3:1 non-text floor on these tones (4.85:1 worst case). White at 85% alpha is 3.92:1 and would still pass, but there is no reason to spend it — a 2px sparkline on a saturated ground is already the thinnest thing on the tile.

markSoft.use: the sparkline area wash, the unfilled remainder of a gauge ring, the resting fill of .jrk-stat__action
markSoft.$note: 1.56-1.64:1 on the four tones, i.e. DECORATIVE ONLY and nothing may depend on seeing it. That is legal here for one specific reason per consumer: the area wash sits under a solid-white line that carries the shape; the gauge remainder is the complement of an arc whose value is printed as text inside the ring; the action button's fill is a hit-target hint on a control that also has an accessible name and a focus ring. Solid white reads 3.11:1 against this fill, so the arc is still separable from its own track. Same value in both themes because it composites onto the tone, not onto the page.

markSoftHover.$note: The one place a vivid tile can use a wash step for feedback rather than a shadow: a shadow is invisible on a saturated ground in both themes, so the light/dark split that .jrk-card--interactive needs does not apply. Lifts 1.30:1 off markSoft.

hover.use: hover on a whole vivid SURFACE — the .jrk-expander--vivid summary. Laid as a flat first background layer over the 135deg ramp, never as a fill that replaces it.
hover.$note: NOT markSoftHover, and the difference is area. markSoft/markSoftHover are the resting and hover fills of .jrk-stat__action, a 24px circle, where 0.28 -> 0.40 white reads as a control lighting up. Spread that 0.28 across a whole card header and the tile changes tone rather than acknowledging the pointer, and it looks like a fifth colour in a four-tone system. 0.10 is the step that reads as feedback at that size. Measured by hand across all four ramps at both stops, because nothing in validate can see a colour inside an rgba() string, let alone one composited over a gradient: 1.19:1 on gradient.blue.from (the shallowest, and the tone the component defaults to), 1.26:1 on violet.from and teal.to, i.e. a band of 1.19-1.26:1. Compare .jrk-card--interactive's dark hover at 1.125:1 — this is the same order of signal, and it is a hover step rather than a state, so it does not owe 3:1.
hover.$oneValueNote: The same value in both themes, which is the rule for this namespace rather than an exception to it: every gradient stop is theme-independent because a vivid surface brings its own ground, so a veil composited onto it is theme-independent too. That is precisely what overlay.hoverVeil CANNOT be — see its note — and the two tokens exist separately for that one reason. Do not collapse them.

focus.use: focus ring for anything inside a vivid tile
focus.$note: focus.ring is #0069d9, which is the blue tone's own light stop — a focus ring that vanishes on one of the four tiles is a keyboard path with a hole in it, and nothing in the base ring's own gating would have caught it because it measures against page, card and well, none of which a vivid tile is. White is 4.85:1 at worst and clears the 3:1 signifier floor on every tone.

gradient.$noControlsNote: A vivid tile takes NO .jrk-btn of any volume. --cta is filled accent.solid, which IS gradient.blue.from, so on the blue tile it is a rectangle of the tile's own colour; --primary is filled accent.wash, a pale tint that on a saturated ground reads as a hole rather than a control. Both are the same failure the hard rules already state for charts ('never put a chart on an accent wash', 'never let a lone blue series sit beside a --cta'), arriving from the other direction. The one control a vivid tile carries is .jrk-stat__action, which is drawn from this namespace and from nothing else.

status.$comment: Apple system colours for the marks; darkened steps for text, because Apple's own systemGreen/Orange/Yellow fail 4.5:1 as text on white. Reserved meanings — never reused as a chart series, which is why green and red are held out of the categorical palette entirely.

solid.use: fill of the ONE filled destructive button — .jrk-btn--danger-solid, never a status mark
solid.$note: A separate, deeper red from status.critical.mark, and it exists because of a coupling that went unnoticed for three accents. .jrk-btn--danger-solid used to fill with the MARK and label it with accent.onSolid — so the red button's ink direction was decided by the accent, and every accent change moved it silently. Nothing gates it: the validator measures status text on the surface and on the wash, never a label on a mark. Under the pastel it sat at 4.01:1 and would have dropped to 3.55:1 when onSolid went back to white. The mark itself cannot be relabelled white either — #ff3b30 gives white 3.55:1. This value is the shallowest deepening of systemRed where white clears 4.5:1 (5.09:1), and it still reads as the same red at a glance. It sits 3.08:1 on the dark card, so it does not need a border in either mode. Same value both modes for the same reason accent.solid is.

onSolid.$note: Its own token rather than a reach for accent.onSolid or text.inverse. text.inverse is #000000 in dark and would put black on a red button there; accent.onSolid is the coupling this pair was created to break.

focus.$comment: Apple's focus ring is a soft accent halo rather than a hard outline. base.css draws it as a 3px ring at reduced alpha plus a 1px solid core.

ring.use: focus ring core — must clear 3:1 on page, card, and inset well
ring.$lightNote: The brand anchor itself, which under the pastel accent was an accessibility failure rather than a style choice (#9ee4ff is 1.40:1 on the card). A focus ring is the single most load-bearing signifier in a keyboard path, so it takes the anchor only because the anchor measures: 5.22:1 card, 5.22:1 on the flat white page, 4.68:1 on a #f2f2f7 inset well (surface.subtle, which is the darkest light surface a ring lands on now that the page is white). Dark takes accent.text at 6.37:1 on the darkest of the three.

offset.use: ring offset, so the ring reads on any surface
offset.$darkNote: Names surface.default and has to move with it — was #1c1c1e.

overlay.$comment: Colours laid OVER a fill rather than selected against one — the full-viewport washes a thing in the top layer drops on the page, plus the hover veil. Nothing in the validator measures this namespace — it iterates surface/text/status/accent/focus/chart by name — so, exactly as with the border namespace, the figures are recorded by hand here and must be re-measured if a page or card value moves.

hoverVeil.use: hover on a surface whose fill is a TINT rather than a plane — the .jrk-expander--pastel summary. Laid as a flat first background layer over the wash.
hoverVeil.$note: The third answer to the problem .jrk-card--interactive:hover and gradient.hover each solve differently, and it exists because neither of theirs applies to a tinted fill. surface.cardHover is wrong (the surface is not a plane, so there is no next plane to step to); shadow.lg is wrong on its own (invisible in dark, which is where the tint is dark and the step is hardest to see anyway); and a single white veil is wrong (it lifts a dark tint 1.34:1 and a light one 1.03:1, so the same interaction would be strong at night and absent by day). So this token is DIRECTIONAL: it darkens a light tint and lightens a dark one, which is the one thing that steps any tint away from itself in both themes. Measured by hand over the four chart.tint slots this component uses (1, 3, 5, 6) — light 1.10:1 (tint-3, the palest) to 1.17:1 (tint-1); dark 1.19:1 (tint-1) to 1.26:1 (tint-3). Same order as .jrk-card--interactive's 1.125:1 dark fill step.
hoverVeil.$alphaNote: The two alphas are not a value and its inverse: 0.045 black and 0.06 white were each solved to land the band in the same place, because a black veil on a pale tint moves luminance faster than a white veil on a deep one. Re-solve both if either moves.
hoverVeil.$reachNote: Nothing stops this from being used on any tinted fill, and that is the intent — status washes, accent.wash, chart tints. What it must NOT be used on is a plane: surface.default/subtle/raised all have a named hover token already, and reaching for a veil there gives a value nothing measures in place of one the validator gates.

scrim.use: .jrk-modal::backdrop — mute the page because the reader is meant to stop looking at it
scrim.$note: Extracted verbatim from the raw rgba() that feedback.css carried inline, so the modal renders byte-identically; this is a de-duplication, not a restyle. Deliberately the SAME value in both themes, which is not the house rule and is not defended — it is pre-existing behaviour left untouched. It inherits the ceiling documented on overlay.spotlight: in dark this wash separates surfaces by 1.17:1 and cannot do better. That is survivable for a modal, whose panel is centred, hairlined and shadowed and does not ask the reader to find a hole. Do not copy this token's untheming to anything that does.

spotlight.use: .jrk-spotlight__cutout — the wash the spotlight hole is punched out of
spotlight.$note: The two alphas are NOT a light value and a flipped copy: each was solved so the SURROUNDING page text lands at the same 4.09:1 residual — 0.60 takes light from 21.00:1, 0.54 takes dark from 15.48:1. Equal suppression, per-theme values, one mechanism. 4.09:1 rather than something heavier is a scope decision: this overlay TEACHES a number in place, so the page around it has to stay readable as the number's context. That is the whole difference from overlay.scrim, which mutes because the reader is meant to look away.
spotlight.$ceilingNote: THE IMPORTANT ONE. A scrim cannot make a hole read as a hole in dark mode, and no alpha fixes it. Against the flat white page this wash separates the spotlit card at 4.76:1; against the #141416 dark page it manages 1.17:1, and scrimming all the way to pure black only reaches 1.34:1 — because the dark card (#232326) is itself nearly black, so there is no room underneath it. Measured across alpha 0.5/0.6/0.7 and pure black at 0.6/0.72/0.8, dark never left the 1.17-1.31 band. So the cutout does NOT rely on this token to be found: .jrk-spotlight__cutout also draws a 2px border.accent ring, which is 5.22:1 on the light page and 8.41:1 on the dark one. The ring is additive in light where the wash already works, and load-bearing in dark where it cannot. This is the same shape as .jrk-card--interactive:hover needing both a shadow and a fill — two channels, each doing the whole job in exactly one theme — and the ring is drawn in BOTH themes rather than dark-only, per the conflict register's rule to pay the redundant ink instead of splitting the mechanism by theme. If the ring is ever dropped from the light rule as 'redundant', dark mode loses its only boundary.

chart.$comment: Data-viz layer. Categorical order is the CVD-safety mechanism — assign slots 1..N in order, NEVER cycle. A 9th series folds into 'Other' or facets. Scatter/bubble/choropleth/small-multiples cap at 3 series (all-pairs validated).

categorical.$derivation: Seeded from Apple's system colours, then ordered by search to maximise the WORST ADJACENT pair across BOTH modes jointly — only neighbours touch in a stack or a line chart, and the slot->hue mapping has to be one fact or a series would change hue when the theme is toggled. Apple publishes no CVD-safe categorical sequence (systemRed beside systemGreen is the textbook protan collapse), so the order is derived, not adopted. Blue is pinned to slot 1: it is the default single-series colour used by every bar list, cell bar and sparkline, so it has to be the neutral one — the unconstrained optimum put orange there, which reads as a warning. systemGreen and systemRed are held out entirely (status good/critical — a green or red series in a financial chart reads as a verdict) and systemIndigo is held out as the UI accent. Result: worst adjacent CVD deltaE 16.3 light / 15.1 dark, roughly double the previous palette.
categorical.$accentReservationStale: The derivation above holds systemIndigo out of the palette 'as the UI accent'. That reservation has been stale since the accent left indigo, and the ACCEPTED debt is now at its worst: the accent is a blue at hue 212deg, and slot 1 is systemBlue at 211deg. They are the same hue. Two earlier readings of this note recorded the gap as 14.6deg (cyan accent vs slot 1) and 7.6deg (cyan accent vs slot 7 teal); it is now about 1deg, against the ONE slot that matters most, because slot 1 is the default single-series colour used by every bar list, cell bar and sparkline. This was a deliberate call, not an oversight: re-deriving the order means re-running the joint light/dark CVD search across all eight slots and re-colouring every chart in the product, and Apple's own consoles ship blue bars beside blue buttons. What separates them is LIGHTNESS only — accent.solid #0069d9 gives white 5.22:1, slot 1 #007aff gives white 4.02:1 — which is a real but thin distinction, thinner than the one the cyan accent had. Consequences to respect until it is resolved: never put a chart on an accent wash; never let a chart's single blue series sit adjacent to a primary button in the same tile without a label between them; and if a ninth series is ever needed, resolve this properly instead of extending the order.
categorical.$redundancy: Every slot carries THREE channels, not one: hue, dash, and shape. Hue alone is only safe for ADJACENT marks. The order was searched to maximise the worst adjacent pair, and the arithmetic consequence is that similar hues get pushed four slots apart — so every pair that collapses under simulated CVD is (n, n+4): orange|yellow deltaE 0.8, mint|teal 1.8 dark, blue|purple 4.4, pink|brown 3.9, measured Machado 2009 severity 1.0 + CIEDE2000 against a floor of 10. Anything comparing NON-adjacent series needs the second channel. dash and shape are assigned so all four (n, n+4) pairs and the (2,4) pair differ in both.
categorical.$barsExemptNote: Bars deliberately have no per-slot channel. .jrk-bars is single-series (slot 1) and .jrk-stack-bar segments are adjacent by construction, so hue alone is sufficient there and the existing 45/135 texture alternation is the right shape for it — chart.css restricts hatching to those two angles because horizontal and vertical read as gridlines, which leaves too few textures to separate (n, n+4) anyway. If a GROUPED bar chart is ever added it puts slot 2 beside slot 4, and it must carry direct labels or the shape channel; alternating texture cannot save it, because n and n+4 always share parity.
categorical.$dashNote: Slot 1 is solid on purpose: it is the default single-series colour and a lone chart must not look provisional. Dash applies to line marks only, and only under the redundancy switch — charts.md reserves dashed strokes for .jrk-threshold, so a dashed SERIES line is legal only where the author opted in. See the conflict register in philosophy.md.

slots.apple: systemYellow, darkened into the lightness band
systemBrown, chroma raised to clear the floor

reliefRequired.note: Sub-3:1 on the white card. Apple's system colours are bright, and a white card is the least forgiving surface for them. Ship visible direct labels or the table view when these are fills. Not dismissable.

tint.$comment: Pastel fills for LARGE marks whose identity is already carried by an axis label, a direct value label, or a number in the legend. Deliberately outside the lightness band and under the chroma floor, so they cannot do identity work and the validator skips them. Using a tint where color IS the identity channel is a bug no gate will catch.
tint.rule: legal only when the mark is axis-labelled, direct-labelled, or accompanied by a value in the legend

ink.use: label set inside a tint fill

ordinalFloor.note: Ordinal ramps must clear 2:1 vs surface. The white card is less forgiving than a tinted one, so the light floor sits deeper than it would on a grey page.

diverging.note: systemRed <-> systemBlue with a NEUTRAL grey midpoint. Equal step count per arm. Never a hue at the midpoint, never a rainbow.

steps.$comment: Four steps per arm, for tinting a TABLE CELL by signed value (.jrk-cell-heat). The poles above are mark colours for a chart; these are fills that sit UNDER text, which is a different job with a harder constraint. Red<->blue rather than red<->green is the whole reason this pair exists: red beside green is the textbook protan collapse, and polarity is exactly the signal you cannot afford to lose. Derived and gated, not eyeballed — `validate` measures all four properties below and fails on any of them.
steps.$constraint: A heat cell carries its own number, so text.primary must clear 4.5:1 on EVERY step in BOTH themes. That is what caps the ramp's darkness in light and its lightness in dark, and it is why neither arm ever reaches its pole: the light arm stops at #ff9c93 (black 10.43:1) and the dark arm at #2f68a1 (#ebebf0 at 4.89:1, the binding value in this whole block). Push either arm one step further for 'more contrast' and the number inside it goes illegible.
steps.$separation: Polarity must survive CVD, because on a signed table the arm IS the meaning. Worst pair is rank 1 in light at deltaE 13.0 (protanopia); every other rank runs 19.5 -> 38.8. Rank 1 was deliberately re-stepped from a paler pair that measured 9.8 and sat under the floor of 10 — the near-zero band is where polarity matters least, but an exception there would still have been an exception.
steps.$rampVsIdentity: Do NOT apply the categorical CVD floor to CONSECUTIVE steps within an arm — they run deltaE 4.2-6.5 and that is correct, not a failure. Adjacent steps in a magnitude ramp are supposed to be similar; that similarity is what makes it read as a ramp. The floor exists for categorical identity, where a reader must name which series a mark belongs to. Here the reader decodes magnitude across the range and the exact value is printed in the cell.

chrome.$comment: surface is the CARD, not the page — that is what chart marks sit on and what the validator measures against.

surface.$darkNote: Was #1c1c1e, left behind when surface.default.dark was lifted. This one is not only a measurement — chart.css strokes it as the 2px ring around .jrk-dot, whose job is to read as a GAP where a dot crosses a line. A ring painted #1c1c1e on a #232326 card is darker than the card, so instead of a gap every dot in dark mode wore a faint dark outline. Nothing failed a gate because a ring is not text and not a mark. Keep this equal to color.surface.default.

family.$comment: Inter first, everywhere. SF Pro cannot be shipped — no webfont, and the outlines are Apple's — so the previous SF-first stack meant Apple hardware and Windows rendered in different typefaces, and the tracking below could only be right for one of them. Inter is the closest widely-available SF analogue and it is the one the library is now tuned against. -apple-system and 'Segoe UI' stay as fallbacks so a failed font load degrades to the platform UI face rather than to Arial. Delivery is css/fonts.css.
family.sans: Inter, 'Inter var', -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif
family.mono: ui-monospace, 'SF Mono', SFMono-Regular, Menlo, 'JetBrains Mono', Consolas, monospace

feature.$comment: Inter carries SF-ish alternates behind OpenType features; base.css applies this on body so every consumer gets the same shapes. cv05 gives lowercase l a tail, which is the one that earns its keep here — property codes and unit numbers are full of l / I / 1 and Inter's default straight l is ambiguous in all three. ss03 rounds the quotes and commas. Both are silently ignored by a font that lacks them, so the fallbacks in family.sans stay safe. Tabular figures are NOT set here — they are per-context via .jrk-tabular, because a standalone hero figure reads better proportional.

size.$comment: Apple's type ladder adapted for a dense desktop dashboard. md (14px) is body.

tracking.$comment: Negative tracking on display sizes is most of what makes type read as Apple. SF tightens optically as it grows and Inter does too — its opsz axis (14..32, requested in css/fonts.css) is what does it — so these values carry over from the SF-first stack unchanged. Do not add more negative tracking to compensate for Inter; opsz and these tokens already stack.

radius.$comment: Softened 2026-08-13 from the tight Apple ladder (4/6/10/12/16) to 6/10/14/18/24. This is a deliberate reversal of the note this comment replaces, which read: 'Apple corners are TIGHTER than most web design systems — macOS controls sit near 6px and cards near 10-12px. The previous 10/14/18/24 read as friendly-web, not Apple.' That was an accurate description of macOS and it is no longer the target. Friendly-web IS the brief now, and radius is the cheapest, highest-coverage lever for it — every control, badge and menu in the library resolves one of these five values, so the whole surface moves together from one edit. Note the ladder is almost exactly the one that was rejected before; the argument that removed it was 'this is not Apple', which is a premise, not a measurement, and the premise changed.
radius.$tilesAreSquareNote: READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING THE SENTENCE ABOVE. It replaces a note dated 2026-08-14 that read 'EVERY TILE IS radius.none NOW' and stated the rule as 'a thing laid ON the page is square, a thing floating ABOVE it is rounded'. THAT SPLIT IS GONE, reversed by direction on 2026-08-18: every tile is radius.md again — .jrk-card, .jrk-stat, both .jrk-stat-row forms, .jrk-chart-card, .jrk-table-wrap, .jrk-sheet, .jrk-alert, and .jrk-expander by composition. So the ladder's 'highest-coverage lever' claim in the comment above is true again, and this note exists only to stop the squaring being re-derived from the component headers, which still discuss it. md, not the radius.xl the tiles carried BEFORE the squaring: 18px was the friendly-web end of the ladder and the brief is a rounded corner, not a lozenge. Do not 'restore' xl on the grounds that this reverts a revert. TWO THINGS ARE STILL NOT ON THE TILE VALUE, and neither was part of either direction. Controls and chips resolve their own rungs — buttons and fields (a text field stays laddered because a fully-rounded one curls in on its first glyph), badges, tags, status chips, and interior chrome inside a tile (the expander's icon chip at md, the sheet's block number at sm). And the overlay surfaces keep the values they have always had — .jrk-modal at 2xl, .jrk-menu, .jrk-hovercard, .jrk-tooltip, .jrk-nav-flyout, .jrk-spotlight at xl. xl is referenced by exactly one component (spotlight); do not delete it as unused. The single surviving radius.none is `.jrk-expander .jrk-expander__panel .jrk-table-wrap`, which is deliberate — see expander.css.
radius.$dataEndNote: NOT part of the softening, and it is the one value in this block that must stay tight. It rounds the loaded end of a bar in .jrk-bars and .jrk-stack-bar, where the corner eats length off the encoding — the mark is the measurement, so a 10px round on a 12px-tall bar visibly shortens the value it is drawing. It stayed at 4px while everything around it grew, which will look like an oversight and is not.

shadow.$comment: Softer and WIDER as of 2026-08-13. The old set was built on 'Apple leans on hairlines and material, not drop shadows' and was deliberately faint and tight (1-4px blurs). The refresh puts white cards on a tinted page, which is a look that reads through ambient shadow rather than through a hairline alone, so the light blurs are roughly tripled at similar or lower opacity — diffuse and low-contrast, not a hard drop. The tint is #10151c rather than pure black: a neutral-cool shadow on a #f5f5f7 page reads as depth, where pure black reads as dirt.
shadow.$darkComment: Dark values are UNCHANGED and stay tight and near-opaque. The reasoning is unchanged with them: in dark the lightened surface and the hairline are the primary elevation cues, and a shadow on a #141416 page barely renders at all — widening the dark blurs would spend nothing and buy nothing. This is the usual shape here (a channel that does the whole job in one theme and nothing in the other), so do not 'restore symmetry' by matching the light values.

card.use: the RESTING elevation of .jrk-card and the chrome that behaves like one — topbar, sheet, auth panel, table panel
card.$note: New on 2026-08-13, and it reversed a standing decision: shadow.lg used to be 'the interactive-card hover raise as well as the popover elevation', under a rule that elevation is opt-in at rest because 'a dashboard of tiles reads calmer flat'. That look is now the brief. This token exists so the reversal is one value rather than a shadow.lg sprinkled onto card rules, and so RESTING and HOVER stay two separate facts. The -5px spread on the second layer keeps the ambient blur tucked under the tile instead of haloing it.
card.$liftNote: DEEPENED 2026-08-14, by instruction — every card floats more. Was `0 1px 2px 0.04, 0 6px 16px -4px 0.06`. Taking y-offset x alpha on the ambient layer as a rough visual weight, that is 0.36 -> 0.81, i.e. the resting float is a bit over twice what it was. The lift could not be spent on this token alone, and that is the part worth reading: the hover step was shadow.lg at weight 1.20, so deepening rest to 0.81 would have closed a 3.3x gap to 1.5x and a hovered card would have stopped visibly answering the pointer — the exact failure $shadowUsageNote names. shadow.lg could not simply grow with it either, because it is ALSO the menu/popover/toast elevation, so growing it would have restyled every popover in the product to lift a card. The fix was structural rather than numeric: see shadow.cardRaise.
card.$darkNote: `none` ON PURPOSE, so a dark card is bounded by exactly what bounded it before: the 1.17:1 fill step plus the hairline. A black ambient shadow on a #141416 page is invisible, so a dark value here would be ink spent on nothing — and if it were pushed dark enough to render, it would read as a smear rather than as a lift. Measured, since it comes up every time someone asks for more lift: black at full strength over the #141416 page tops out at 1.14:1, and a realistic blurred ambient layer lands near 1.07:1. There is no alpha that buys a visible dark shadow, so the 2026-08-14 lift is LIGHT-ONLY BY CONSTRUCTION. Dark's elevation channel is the fill step, which is why .jrk-card--interactive:hover carries surface.cardHover as well and why that declaration is not redundant.

cardRaise.use: a card lifted ABOVE its resting plane — .jrk-card--interactive:hover / :focus-visible, and .jrk-card--raised
cardRaise.$note: Added 2026-08-14 to make the resting lift on shadow.card possible. The card ladder and the popover ladder used to COLLIDE on shadow.lg — a hovered card and an open menu were the same elevation — and that collision is what made a deeper resting card impossible to express: any value that restored the hover gap also restyled every popover. They are two ladders now. CARDS: shadow.card (0.81) -> shadow.cardRaise (2.70). POPOVERS: shadow.lg (1.20) -> shadow.xl (4.32) for modals. Weights are y-offset x alpha on the ambient layer, the same rough measure used throughout this namespace. The card ladder keeps its original 3.3x gap, which is the number to preserve if either end ever moves again. shadow.lg now sits BETWEEN the two card steps and that is not a problem: it is a small surface with a hairline that never sits beside a card at rest.
cardRaise.$darkNote: shadow.lg's dark value VERBATIM, which is deliberate and is not laziness. Dark elevation is carried by surface.cardHover's 1.125:1 fill step; the shadow is close to invisible there, so this value's job in dark is only to not regress what .jrk-card--interactive:hover already had when it pointed at shadow.lg.
